title: Patriot missiles have been a godsend for Ukraine against Putin, but they’re running out. Kyiv needs help and fast | Jack Watling
summary:
Europe and Nato have known for years that interceptor production can’t keep up with demand and now disaster looms, putting us all in danger

“Invincible.” That was how Vladimir Putin described Russia’s latest generation of ballistic missiles in 2018. In 2022 he would unleash this arsenal to strike across Ukraine, hitting command centres, critical infrastructure and airfields. Then, in 2023, Ukraine received Patriot air defence systems from its international partners. The US-supplied missile interceptor would prove to be an effective shield against Russian strikes.

But this year, supplies of Patriot missiles have run out and Kyiv has suffered the consequences. Intercepts have gone from more than 70% to none, so that night after night Russia strikes Ukraine’s infrastructure with impunity. This tragedy was long foretold, and there are no quick fixes.

Jack Watling is senior research fellow for applied military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute

title: Ukrainian cathedrals, Gaza’s archives, Iranian squares – modern war is systematically erasing human history | Simon Jenkins
summary:
It is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage too

Wars may not take summer holidays, but they do sometimes see exhaustion. As drones race back and forth across Ukraine and the strait of Hormuz, a grim stalemate seems to have invaded the earth beneath. Aerial bombardment knows limited resistance and even less victory or defeat. Ukraine, Russia, Israel, Iran and their allies seem able to defy diplomacy and drop bombs on each other for ever.

At which point the outside world can merely count some of the costs. Vladimir Putin’s known desire to eliminate Ukraine’s historical identity has led to its cultural devastation. Two weeks ago Unesco reported the destruction or dereliction of 545 of its historic buildings, including 156 religious sites and 43 museums. The attempted eradication of what Putin himself claims to be an intrinsic part of Russia’s own history is sickening.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

title: I got married in the Vegas of Europe. It was the most romantic 20 minutes of my life | Jules Darmanin
summary:
Post-Brexit visa rules and faceless pen-pushers were keeping me and my partner apart. But love finds a way

Consider your ideal wedding. You may picture religious pageantry, majestic domes and the auspicious light of the Divine beaming on a white dress. Maybe you see friends dancing on a pub’s veranda, cheering for you in front of a town hall, or anywhere really – the people you love are there, and it’s all that matters.

What you are probably not picturing is a meet-up with Chris and Mitch, two complete strangers waiting for you and your future spouse by a nondescript fountain in the middle of Copenhagen. Judging by my soon-to-be-wife’s bewildered laugh throughout the entire 20 minutes of our wedding, this is not what she was picturing either. Should I add that neither of us is Danish, or lives in Denmark?

Jules Darmanin is a French journalist

title: Ceuta showed just how easily Europe can be divided
summary:
The migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken note

Within hours of the first pictures of tens of thousands of migrants swimming the short distance from Morocco to the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta hitting social media on 30 July, 22 European Union leaders, the Trump administration and Israel had piled on to criticise Madrid.

The outbreak of hysteria and recrimination was a case study in 21st-century politics, driven by real-time images in a media echo chamber where populists set the agenda on migration, propagating fear, prejudice and demagogic proposals. Above all, the kneejerk reactions undermined trust between European allies and dealt a setback to EU efforts to jointly manage migration, counter people-smuggling and resist the weaponisation of migrants by non-EU countries.

Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy warns Egypt of food supply threat caused by Russian strikes in Black Sea
summary:
Kyiv says exports to Egypt under threat from Russian attacks; Moscow dismisses idea of Black Sea ceasefire. What we know on day 1,635

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned Egyptian counterpart Abdel ⁠Fattah al-Sisi of possible food supply shortages caused by Russian strikes on ⁠cargo vessels in the Black Sea. “Ukraine is one of ⁠the largest food suppliers to ​Egypt and to ‌a significant number ‌of other countries in Africa ‌and the Middle East. These supplies are now under serious threat because of Russia’s war,” Zelenskyy said on X. “We are already seeing ‌a significant reduction in supplies, and this could have very ​unpleasant consequences due to rising prices and shortages,” he said, adding that the two countries had agreed to ⁠work on solutions.

Russia on Friday dismissed the idea of a ceasefire ‌with Ukraine in the Black Sea, saying it saw no grounds for “half-measures” that would ​offer a respite to the other side. In a statement, foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine of “brazen acts of terrorism” against shipping, while making no ⁠mention of Russia’s own attacks. “We view these attacks (by Ukraine) as a ​deliberate policy aimed at destabilising civilian ‌shipping in the Black ‌Sea region,” Zakharova said. “At the same time, we see no signs of improvement in the situation and, consequently, no grounds for half-measures that merely grant the Kyiv regime a temporary breathing space.”

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks in recent weeks against commercial ships in the ​Black Sea, driving world grain prices higher. Zakharova’s comments followed an earlier Ukraine proposal for both sides to halt their attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea in an apparent attempt to reopen a crucial grain corridor. Kyiv is said to have made the offer through a third party.

Russia has intensified its online disinformation campaign in Poland, using a dispute between Warsaw and Kyiv over second world war massacres ⁠to inflame tensions between Ukraine and ⁠its key ally, Polish ​officials and researchers say. The messaging, mostly posted on social media accounts in Polish, also tries to foment anger in Poland against refugees, as opinion polls show support for the far-right growing ahead of closely contested ⁠parliamentary elections in 2027.

The long-running second world war dispute between Poland and Ukraine centres on the Volhynia massacres, in which Poland says Ukrainians killed about 100,000 Poles between 1943 and 1945. The dispute intensified after ⁠Zelenskyy named an army unit after insurgents who perpetrated the massacres, prompting hard-right president Karol Nawrocki to strip his Ukrainian counterpart of a top Polish ​honour in June.

Russian authorities acknowledged Friday that some regions face new petrol shortages, as Ukraine continues to attack the country’s oil refineries to blunt Russia’s capacity to pursue the war. Russia has shut down one big refinery at Orsk – about 1,300km (810 miles) from the frontline – for six months after it was attacked this week. “The situation remains tense in several regions of the country regarding fuel supplies to service stations,” the government said in a social media post. Oil companies are “taking the necessary measures to increase deliveries to the most vulnerable regions”, it said.

Russian jet-powered drones have struck a home in northern Ukraine, killing a 29-year-old woman and her 9-year-old son. This attack comes after the United Nations reported that July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since the early weeks of Russia’s invasion. At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 wounded last month. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drones have targeted Russian infrastructure, including a major port north of Moscow.

Romania found ⁠a second drone in national ⁠territory on ⁠Friday, ​in the south-eastern village ⁠of Plauru near the Danube border with ⁠Ukraine, the defence ​ministry said ‌on ‌Friday, after a ‌low flying drone undetected by radar systems crashed earlier. The ministry did not specify ‌the origins of the drone. ​The Nato state has seen Russian drones repeatedly breach ⁠its airspace over the ​last four ​years.

Russian president Vladimir Putin told North Korean ⁠leader Kim Jong-un that Moscow and Pyongyang were cooperating across all areas to ensure ⁠regional ​security and stability, North Korean state media KCNA reported on Saturday. Putin said in a message ⁠to Kim marking the anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japanese colonial rule that he was confident Russia and ⁠North Korea would continue “constructive joint work” on bilateral and international ​issues, KCNA said. Kim had ‌visited Pyongyang’s Liberation ‌Tower on Friday to pay tribute to Soviet soldiers who fought ‌Japan in the second world war, KCNA reported.
